## {{< fa circle-info >}} What happens in the workshop

In this workshop we build one dataset together. Every participant contributes to it through GitHub, a little before the conference (step 2 below) and the rest in the room, and the contributions arrive as different kinds of raw data.

I then run the workflow live with the free, open source tool [washr]({{< var tools.washr >}}), from these raw files to a data package and its website. A coding agent performs the steps. The points where a person confirms stay visible, and so does the record of what the AI did and of who contributed what. You review the documentation and propose changes on GitHub. In groups we then discuss four themes the workflow raises for data curation.

The workshop does not teach GitHub. We use two elements of it, issues and comments, and with them you learn how to contribute to a project on GitHub. The abstract is in the [conference record]({{< meta cohort.record_url >}}).

## {{< fa route >}} From raw file to website

A dataset passes through six stages on its way to a published data package and website.

1.  **Raw data.** The file as it was collected, often an Excel sheet. It is kept as it is and never overwritten.
2.  **Analysis ready data.** Code cleans the raw file and saves a tidy copy. Raw data, code and tidy data sit in one public repository, so everyone can see how one became the other.
3.  **Documentation and metadata.** A data dictionary explains every column. A citation file names everyone who contributed, and metadata describes the dataset in a form that programs read.
4.  **Review.** A check finds what is missing or inconsistent before anything is published.
5.  **Release and DOI.** A release files a permanent copy in the Zenodo archive and gives the dataset a DOI, the link others cite.
6.  **Website.** The data package gets its own website with the documentation, the data dictionary and download buttons. This is the part made for humans.

## {{< fa bullseye >}} Learning objectives

After the workshop, you can

1.  describe the stages a raw dataset passes through on its way to a published data package and website;
2.  contribute to a shared dataset on GitHub with issues and comments, and propose a change that way;
3.  tell which steps of data curation a coding agent can take over, which stay with the researcher, and how AI contributions are recorded.

## {{< fa comments >}} Discussion themes

The workflow raises four questions, technical, organisational, societal and ethical. Four groups take one theme each. Each group answers the question of its theme, writes down on sticky notes the two main challenges it sees and one recommendation for researchers or institutions, and one person per group reports back to the room.

-   **Oversight.** Publishers sell AI curated data publication on closed platforms. How much the author still checks is unclear. In our workflow every AI step is visible. Which curation steps must a person confirm, and who checks that it happened?
-   **Disclosure.** We record how AI contributed to each output, in commit trailers and a prompt archive. The record for this workshop, from the proposal to the slides, is public. What does a reader of a published dataset need to know about the AI contribution, and how much record keeping can be asked of a researcher?
-   **Sensitive data.** Ours comes from households in low income countries. What may enter a public repository, and when only aggregates may be released, is half-solved for us. Where is the line between what an agent may see and what may be published?
-   **Rewards.** With AI, a paper is drafted in a day from well curated data. Scientific credit should shift towards the data. Argue back.

rawtoweb is a workshop of [{{< var department >}}]({{< var author-url >}}), {{< var institute >}}. In 75 minutes the room builds one dataset together, and it becomes a data package in front of the room, documented, versioned, with a data dictionary and a website. A coding agent does the mechanical work with the free, open source tools [washr]({{< var tools.washr >}}) and [pkgreview]({{< var tools.pkgreview >}}), and every human and every AI step stays visible in the record.

## {{< fa route >}} How a workshop runs

1.  **Before the day.** Participants take a survey and make a first contribution to the workshop dataset on GitHub, which tests the account they need.
2.  **On the day.** An introduction to the workflow, the dataset built together and turned into a data package and its website in a live run with washr, a discussion on four themes in groups, and the take home.
3.  **Afterwards.** Participants who want to publish a dataset of their own this way get a follow-up. The repositories stay public. The pages of a workshop are frozen when it is over, so what a group saw stays as it was.

## {{< fa comments >}} The four themes

Every workshop ends with the same four questions: oversight of AI curation, disclosure of AI contributions, sensitive data, and scientific credit for data.
